headline: PLS.AX gets hammered -5% on lithium weakness while GTA VI pre-orders open today — big day for your TTWO holding.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara dropped nearly 5% today in a rough session for lithium stocks broadly. Lithium prices remain under pressure as the global supply glut continues, and analysts are questioning whether PLS's big P2000 expansion spend is smart strategy or a risk at these low prices. The stock is now down over 20% on your total investment.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO slipped 2.83% in last night's session despite massive GTA VI news — Rockstar officially announced pre-orders open today (June 25) ahead of a November 19 launch. The dip looks like profit-taking after the stock had already run up on GTA VI hype. The underlying catalyst (pre-orders live, release date confirmed) is very positive for the stock medium-term.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft fell 2.27% last night, one of the bigger drags on the NASDAQ. No major company-specific news drove the move — it looks like broader tech selling pressure. MSFT is now down 17.5% on your total investment, sitting at $365.46 USD.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI had a strong session today, up 2.73% on the ASX. AI-related stocks continue to attract interest, with ongoing news around chip development (Broadcom partnering with OpenAI on a new AI processor) keeping the sector in favour. Still slightly underwater overall at -2.3% on your investment.

movers.name: BetaShares Global Energy ETF
movers.note: FUEL slipped 1.23% today as oil prices continue to ease. Crude (WTI) is sitting around $69.89/barrel after falling as more tankers have resumed moving through the Strait of Hormuz (a key oil shipping route in the Middle East), reducing supply fears that had been propping prices up.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS edged up 0.68% today on the ASX, tracking the resilience in US markets from last night's session. A solid hold — up 2.96% on your total investment.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE gained 0.51% today, a quiet but positive session for emerging markets. Only marginally in the green overall (+0.6% on your investment).

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG crept up 0.17% today — a very steady session for this diversified fund. Up 2.19% on your total investment, doing its job as a slow-and-steady core holding.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOG barely moved last night, slipping just 0.3% to $345.04 USD. No specific news drove the dip — it was a quiet session for the stock. Still up 12.2% on your total investment, the best performer in the portfolio.

watch_today.title: GTA VI Pre-Orders Open TODAY — TTWO in focus
watch_today.detail: Rockstar Games officially opened GTA VI pre-orders today (June 25) with a confirmed November 19 launch date. Investor's Business Daily just slapped a fresh Buy rating on Take-Two ahead of this. The stock dipped 2.83% last night which looks like pre-event jitter — the actual pre-order numbers over the next few days will be the real signal. This is the biggest catalyst for TTWO in years.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — Pilbara near pain threshold, watch for further falls
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals dropped nearly 5% today and is now down 20% on your investment. Lithium prices are still weak, analysts are debating whether the stock is overvalued, and the company is ramping up its expensive P2000 expansion. No clear bottom in sight yet. If you have a high pain tolerance and believe in lithium long-term, hold — but know the risk is real.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX riding the AI wave — momentum building
watch_today.detail: GXAI jumped 2.73% today, one of the best performers in your portfolio this session. The AI theme is getting a fresh boost from news that Broadcom is collaborating with OpenAI to build a new AI processor specifically optimised for large language models (the kind that powers ChatGPT). This is a genuine tailwind for AI-focused ETFs like GXAI.

watch_today.title: RBA rate decision looming — watch for another hike
watch_today.detail: This is the big one for Australian investors this week. Today's data showed unemployment dipped again, which actually makes rate hikes *more* likely (a strong jobs market means the RBA doesn't need to ease off). Underlying inflation is also creeping back up. Bond traders aren't ruling out a fourth rate rise. A rate hike would hurt growth stocks and property — keep an eye on how this develops.

watch_today.title: MSFT down 2.27% — holding underwater, no catalyst yet
watch_today.detail: Microsoft had another rough night, down 2.27% with no major news trigger — just broad tech selling. It's now 17.5% in the red on your total investment. There's no strong reason to sell here (the AI story is intact), but equally no near-term catalyst to buy more. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: Oil sliding — FUEL.AX under continued pressure
watch_today.detail: Crude oil is at $69.89/barrel and at a four-month low, as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz (the key Middle East oil shipping route) has improved. This reduces the supply-scare premium that had been supporting prices. FUEL.AX tracks global energy companies, so sustained low oil prices will keep a lid on this ETF. Nothing urgent, but worth watching if oil keeps dropping.

markets.summary: The ASX 200 closed down 0.68% today at 8,748 points — a soft session with no single dramatic catalyst, just general caution around the RBA rate outlook and softer commodity prices. Last night on Wall Street, both the S&P 500 (-0.1%) and NASDAQ (-0.43%) slipped mildly. Gold is the standout, pushing above $4,010 USD/oz, suggesting investors are keeping some money in safe havens. Oil continued to slide toward $69.89/barrel as Middle East shipping risks ease.

politics.summary: The big domestic story today is the RBA — unemployment just dipped again, which ironically increases the chance of another interest rate hike. Meanwhile, the government scored a win in parliament, dumping the so-called 'widow's tax' as part of a broader superannuation reform bill that passed today.

stories.title: Unemployment dips — and that actually makes another rate hike more likely
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's unemployment rate fell again, which sounds like good news but creates a headache for the Reserve Bank. A tight jobs market (meaning lots of people employed) tends to push wages and spending higher, which can keep inflation stubbornly elevated. Economists are now warning that underlying inflation is climbing again, making another RBA rate hike firmly back on the cards. Bond traders aren't even ruling out a fourth rate rise this cycle. If you have a mortgage or own property, this is the number to watch this week.

stories.title: Government dumps 'widow's tax' as super reform bill passes parliament
stories.why_it_matters: The government's superannuation reform bill passed parliament today, and as part of the deal Labor agreed to scrap the so-called 'widow's tax' — a rule that had been reducing superannuation death benefit payments to surviving spouses in certain circumstances. The change is a win for retirees and their families who were being hit by the rule. The broader super reforms still include the controversial changes to tax concessions on large super balances.

stories.title: RBA faces 'make-or-break' jobs data — rate hike decision looming
stories.why_it_matters: Multiple outlets today describe the RBA as facing an 'uncomfortable' call, with the jobs figures released this week described as 'make-or-break' for the rate decision. The RBA has already hiked rates several times this cycle, and the question is whether this latest data forces their hand again. AFR reports bond traders won't rule out a fourth rate hike even as some inflation measures cool. A hike would push up mortgage repayments for anyone on a variable rate home loan.

stories.title: Labor's union procurement changes draw 'corruption risk' warning
stories.why_it_matters: The SMH is reporting that Labor's proposed changes to government procurement rules — which would give unions greater involvement in decisions around government contracts — have been labelled a 'corruption risk written into law' by critics. The concern is that the changes could allow union-affiliated organisations to influence which companies win taxpayer-funded government work. The reforms are controversial and face pushback from business groups and integrity advocates.

ai.summary: Today's AI news is dominated by regulation debates — the UK's financial regulator is sounding the alarm that AI is moving faster than the law can keep up, while Bloomberg and Reason Magazine both have sharp critiques of how governments are (mis)handling AI rules. On the tech side, Broadcom and OpenAI are teaming up to build a custom AI chip.

stories.title: UK financial regulator warns: AI is moving faster than the law
stories.why_it_matters: The head of the UK's Financial Conduct Authority (the body that regulates banks and financial firms) publicly warned this week that artificial intelligence is advancing so rapidly that existing laws simply can't keep pace. The FCA is concerned that AI tools being deployed in financial services — things like automated lending decisions, fraud detection, and trading algorithms — are operating in a legal grey zone. For investors, this means AI-heavy financial businesses face growing regulatory uncertainty, which is both a risk and an opportunity for whoever gets the rules right first.

stories.title: Broadcom and OpenAI team up to build a custom AI chip for large language models
stories.why_it_matters: Broadcom — the US chipmaker — has announced a collaboration with OpenAI (the company behind ChatGPT) to build a new AI processor specifically optimised for large language models (the tech that powers AI chatbots and text generators). This is significant because it signals that AI companies are moving beyond using off-the-shelf chips (like Nvidia's) and building custom silicon tailored to their specific needs. It's a direct challenge to Nvidia's dominance and a big vote of confidence in the AI infrastructure buildout. Good news for AI-themed ETFs like your GXAI.AX.

stories.title: CommBank report: Australia needs AI investment to fix flat productivity
stories.why_it_matters: CommBank released research arguing that Australia's persistently flat productivity (meaning we're not getting more output per hour worked) can't be fixed without serious investment in AI and regulatory reform. The report frames AI adoption not just as a tech story but as an economic necessity for Australia to keep pace globally. For context, flat productivity means slower wage growth and weaker company profits over time — making this directly relevant to long-term investors in Australian equities.

stories.title: The Anthropic saga: why rushed AI regulation can backfire badly
stories.why_it_matters: Bloomberg published a sharp opinion piece using Anthropic (the AI safety company behind the Claude chatbot) as a case study for how not to regulate AI. The argument: well-intentioned rules can end up being captured by the very companies they're meant to regulate, creating barriers for smaller competitors while entrenching the big players. This is the 'self-serving regulation' problem — big AI firms lobby for rules that look tough but are actually written to their advantage. Relevant for investors watching how the regulatory landscape will shape AI industry winners and losers.

sport.summary: NRL Round 17 kicks off tonight at CommBank Stadium with Eels vs Rabbitohs (7:50pm). Big storyline this week: the Bulldogs have reportedly won the race to sign a highly-sought halfback, and the NRL's dream of a Global Round overseas has reportedly been torpedoed by the English Premier League. Wimbledon is also underway, with Djokovic chasing a record 25th Grand Slam.

stories.title: Bulldogs reportedly land highly-sought halfback in major coup
stories.why_it_matters: The Canterbury Bulldogs have reportedly beaten several rival clubs to sign a highly-coveted halfback, representing a significant recruitment win for the club. The article doesn't name the player, but describes it as a 'massive coup' — suggesting it's a marquee half who was attracting attention from multiple NRL clubs. The Bulldogs have been building strongly and this would add another big piece to their roster heading into the second half of the season.

stories.title: How the EPL may have killed the NRL's Global Round dream
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL's ambition to stage a 'Global Round' — playing games overseas to grow the sport internationally — has reportedly hit a major wall. According to the Daily Telegraph, the English Premier League's scheduling and venue dominance in key UK markets has made it practically impossible for the NRL to lock in the stadiums and broadcast windows needed for a viable overseas round. It's a significant blow to the NRL's international growth strategy.

stories.title: Wests Tigers sign replacement for Jarome Luai as club continues rebuild
stories.why_it_matters: The Wests Tigers have continued their busy off-season recruitment drive by signing a halfback to replace Jarome Luai, who departed after the 2025 season. The Tigers have been one of the most active clubs in the market, clearly signalling a commitment to rebuilding under their current coaching setup. The specific signing details weren't named in the headline, but the move suggests the Tigers are trying to address their playmaking depth ahead of 2027.

stories.title: Can Djokovic win a 25th Grand Slam at Wimbledon?
stories.why_it_matters: Wimbledon is underway and the big question is whether Novak Djokovic can claim a record 25th Grand Slam title on the grass at SW19. Djokovic has won Wimbledon 7 times previously and at 39 is still one of the favourites on the surface he knows best. A win would cement his status as the greatest tennis player of all time by the numbers — he's currently tied or ahead of Nadal and Federer in majors count depending on how you count.
